newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Bank Negara intervenes to protect ringgit.
newsitem.headline: Bank Negara intervenes to protect ringgit.

text.p: Malaysia's central bank on Wednesday intervened directly in the foreign exchange market to protect the ringgit after Thailand announced a managed float of the baht, dealers said.

It was the first time in many years that Bank Negara used its own name while intervening in the foreign exchange market. It usually uses a broker or some of Malaysia's biggest banks for its market operations, dealers said.
"Negara came out himself to sell the dollar instead of normal exercise of proxy," said a dealer with a European bank in Singapore.
The intervention followed a sharp weakening in the baht after Thailand announced a managed float for the baht from Wednesday, allowing market forces to set the value of the currency.

Bank Negara bought ringgit at 2.5250 to the dollar, dealers said. The currency had weakened to that level on Wednesday and had tested it several times in the past week. Market players said the 2.5280-2.5300 level was viewed as a stronger barrier.

However, for the time being, Bank Negara's intervention has kept the ringgit from breaking 2.5250, dealers said. The currency was quoted at 2.5234/44 to the dollar at 0600 GMT from an open of around 2.5230/35.
The actual size of the intervention was not known but dealers believed the amount of dollars sold by Bank Negara was small.
No confirmation was available from the central bank, which does not usually comment on its intervention operations.

"Bank Negara will continue to support the ringgit around 2.5250. I think this time around, the central banks (in the region) will be able to defend their currencies," said Dilip Ratha, regional economist with W.I. Carr in Singapore.
He said the spillover effect of the baht float on regional currencies would be brief.
"It was an unexpected move by the Bank of Thailand. There will be some speculative pressure but it will be short-lived," he said.

Economists said after the ringgit came under speculative attack in May, Bank Negara and other regional central banks would not hesitate to show their presence in the market on any sign of an attack on their currencies.
In May, speculators unloaded the ringgit because of Thailand's financial crisis. Bank Negara intervened aggressively to stem the ringgit's losses, but dollar sales were done through agent banks.
The intervention saw the central bank's foreign reserves fall by 1.4 billion ringgit ($555 million) to 69.7 billion ringgit at end-May compared with a fortnight earlier.
Economists were maintaining their forecast of a stronger ringgit in the next six months.
They expect the Malaysian unit to trade at 2.47-2.48 to the dollar by the end of the year on the back of strong economic fundamentals and high interest rates in Malaysia.
The ringgit hit its strongest level in 17 months of 2.4680 on January 13 this year, after ending 1996 at 2.5305.
